rewrite: Sell more to existing customers with a cheap, low-risk setup. (Paraphrase of the Campaign's translation.)
text: increase the share of wallet opportunity through a new capital light and low risk operating model
why: Jargon stacked into noun phrases; no actor, no concrete action.

identified_by: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (NHS England)
rewrite: Groups of healthcare providers working together will help local health systems do their main job. (Paraphrase of the Campaign's translation.)
text: provider collaboratives will be a key component in enabling ICSs to deliver their core purpose
why: Undefined acronym, abstract jargon ('key component', 'deliver their core purpose').

identified_by: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (Pensions Dashboards Programme)
rewrite: We have started buying the main computer system.
text: With our procurement of the principal digital architecture underway
why: Nominalization ('procurement') and inflated words hide a simple action.

identified_by: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (SP Energy Networks)
rewrite: If you own a generator, you must update its protection equipment by 1 September 2022.
text: EREC G59 requirements must be implemented by generation owners
why: Undefined codes; passive voice hides who must act.

rewrite: We're selling fewer products.
text: We are currently in the process of consolidating our product range
why: Filler ('currently in the process of') and euphemism.

identified_by: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (Lloyds pharmacy)
rewrite: Our pharmacists read prescriptions quickly because they know the drugs well.
text: The cognitive process that staff will go through when interpreting prescriptions
why: Abstract, inflated phrasing for a simple claim.

identified_by: Center for Plain Language, Grand WonderMark (Charles Schwab)
text: (Magazine ad in which judges estimated nearly 90% of the language was legalese.)
why: Asked for trust while making it impossible to tell what the firm would do with the reader's money.

identified_by: Center for Plain Language, WonderMark (Department of Homeland Security)
text: (Deferred-action form whose opening paragraph held an 81-word sentence.)
why: Bureaucratic density; a judge said it barely read as English.

identified_by: Center for Plain Language, WonderMark (1&1 Internet)
text: (Webhosting upgrade letter full of technical terms, sent to non-programmer customers.)
why: Wrong audience: a submitter with a law degree couldn't follow it.

identified_by: Denis Dutton, Bad Writing Contest, first prize (Judith Butler, in diacritics)
text: (A one-sentence passage of academic theory built from chains of abstract nouns.)
why: Run by the journal Philosophy and Literature to expose scholarship it called pretentious gibberish. Butler defended the passage in the New York Times.

identified_by: Helen Sword, 'Zombie Nouns,' New York Times
rewrite: Writers who overload their sentences with abstract nouns tend to sound pompous. (Paraphrase of Sword's rewrite.)
text: The proliferation of nominalizations in a discursive formation ...
why: Seven nominalizations, no human actor, no action. Sword built it as a deliberate bad example.

identified_by: Steven Pinker, The Sense of Style
rewrite: Tap someone's wrist, elbow, and shoulder in quick succession, and they feel one tap hopping up the arm.
text: (A psychology-journal sentence about 'stimulus' and 'poststimulus events.')
why: Curse of knowledge: technical abstraction where a concrete description was available.

identified_by: George Orwell, Politics and the English Language
rewrite: I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.
text: (Orwell's parody: Ecclesiastes 9:11 rewritten as abstract 'modern English' about success, failure, and unpredictable factors.)
why: The King James original (public domain) is concrete and visual; the parody replaces every image with abstraction.

rewrite: We applied ...
text: We made an application ...
why: Nominalization with a weak verb.

rewrite: We will not own the company's stock.
text: We will have no stock ownership of the company.
why: Hidden verb ('ownership').

rewrite: This summary highlights some information from this Prospectus.
text: The following summary is intended only to highlight certain information contained elsewhere in this Prospectus.
why: Superfluous words.

rewrite: Only the primary beneficiary may receive these dividends.
text: Persons other than the primary beneficiary may not receive these dividends.
why: Negative turned positive.

rewrite: You must include the following information in your application.
text: The following information must be included in the application for it to be considered complete.
why: Passive to active; addresses the reader as 'you'.

rewrite: We analyze data.
text: We conduct an analysis of the data.
why: Hidden verb.

rewrite: These sections tell you how to meet the requirements of Circular A-110 for this grant program.
text: These sections describe types of information that would satisfy the application requirements of Circular A-110 as it would apply to this grant program.
why: Conditional tense and abstraction replaced with present tense and 'you'.

rewrite: You need an electronic travel authorisation.
text: An electronic travel authorisation is needed.
why: Active voice addressed to the reader.

rewrite: If the cache is full, clear it.
text: Clear it if the cache is full.
why: Condition before instruction.

rewrite: You must configure the rules before you deploy.
text: Configuring the rules is required before deploying.
why: -ing forms and passive replaced with 'you must'.

rewrite: Request only one token.
text: Only request one token.
why: Modifier placed next to what it modifies.

identified_by: Center for Plain Language, Grand ClearMark (Health Literacy Media & Novartis)
text: (Clinical-trial results summary for teens and young adults with diabetes.)
why: Judges praised short sentences, common words, a tone right for young readers without condescension, and regular testing with the audience.

identified_by: Center for Plain Language, ClearMark (Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation)
text: (Patient guide: dietary supplements and myeloma.)
why: A one-sentence 'quick takeaway' at the top, familiar words, short active sentences, basics-to-details order, clear headings.

text: (Health-insurance tax form letter and FAQ, Massachusetts Health Connector.)
why: Opening statement of purpose and required action; logically ordered headings; a checklist that anticipates questions.

identified_by: Center for Plain Language, ClearMark legal category
text: (Proposed rule, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.)
why: A regulation that avoids jargon, uses familiar nouns and active verbs, tables, vertical lists, and question-and-answer headings.

identified_by: Joseph Kimble, survey of Michigan lawyers
text: (Plain-language rewrite of a Michigan judicial opinion.)
why: 61% of 251 lawyers preferred it. Top reasons: less unnecessary detail and an opening summary. Average sentence length fell from 25 to 19 words.

identified_by: Warren Buffett, preface to the SEC Plain English Handbook
text: Write with a specific person in mind.
why: Buffett pictured his sisters: smart, but not experts in finance.

identified_by: A Sun customer, quoted in Morkes & Nielsen's web-writing research (NN/g)
rewrite: Yes, Sun still supports that Solaris version. (Our illustration: answer the question with the fact.)
text: Sun is exceptionally committed to...
why: The customer asked whether Sun would support an older Solaris platform and got self-promotion instead of an answer. They said they wanted fact, not platitudes.

rewrite: If you have any questions, please phone.
text: If there are any points on which you require explanation or further particulars we shall be glad to furnish such additional details as may be required by telephone.
why: Twenty-eight words of formal padding reduce to six.

rewrite: Children need good schools if they are to learn properly.
text: High-quality learning environments are a necessary precondition for facilitation and enhancement of the ongoing learning process.
why: Abstract nouns replaced by the real actors (children) and a concrete noun (schools).

rewrite: (The Campaign's version thanks the writer, then says the library needs to see the posters first to check they won't offend anyone.)
text: (A council's library letter about displaying benefit-rights posters, full of 'provenance and authoritativeness' and 'items of a disputatious or polemic kind'.)
why: The rewrite answers the actual request and states the next step.

rewrite: (The Campaign's version: 'You must now pay a penalty charge of £70 within 28 days', with the exact date, and 'Do not pay the traffic warden'.)
text: (A UK parking ticket: 'must be paid not later than the last day of the period of 28 days beginning with the date on which this PCN was served'.)
why: Addresses the reader as 'you', gives the actual deadline, spells out the abbreviation, and drops the all-caps shouting.

identified_by: Plain English Campaign, Golden Bull (Halton Borough Council)
text: (A 630-word single sentence in a footpath-diversion notice.)
why: One sentence tried to describe an entire route by distances from building corners. A map or numbered steps would do it.

identified_by: Federal Plain Language Guidelines, 'Write short sentences'
rewrite: We prepare a preliminary proposal to present to an employer who agrees to negotiate a job that meets both his and your employment needs.
text: The proposal is presented to an employer who agrees to negotiate an individualized job that meets the employment needs of the applicant and real business needs of the employer.
why: Passive and third person replaced with 'we' and 'you'; the full rewrite also splits the original into shorter sentences.

rewrite: Smoking causes heart disease and lung cancer.
text: Heart disease and lung cancer are caused by smoking.
why: Passive to active.

rewrite: Cook meat until it is not pink in the middle.
text: Following safety precautions can reduce food-borne disease transmission.
why: Vague, passive abstraction replaced by a concrete action.

identified_by: CDC, Simply Put; HHS Health Literacy Online 2.4
rewrite: Wear your helmet every time you ride your bicycle.
text: Do not ride your bicycle without wearing a helmet.
why: Negative instruction turned positive.

rewrite: Wear your seatbelt. It could save your life.
text: Seat Belts
why: One-word label replaced by a complete-idea heading.

rewrite: Feel for lumps about the size of a pea.
text: Feel for lumps about 5 to 6 millimeters in diameter.
why: A familiar comparison instead of a measurement.

rewrite: You may need a test to find out what's wrong.
text: Tests may be needed to find out what's wrong.
why: Passive to active, addressed to the reader.

rewrite: ... A neurologist is a doctor who treats problems related to the brain and nervous system.
text: Your primary doctor may refer you to a neurologist.
why: Defines the term in context, the first time.

rewrite: Check your blood pressure every 2 years, especially if you are age 40 or older.
text: (A definition of blood pressure, then 'get it checked often.')
why: States the behavior first, specifically.

identified_by: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, top 10 tips
rewrite: Store files online, access them from all your devices, and share them with coworkers.
text: You can access Office apps across your devices, and you get online file storage and sharing.
why: Starts with verbs; drops 'you can'.

rewrite: Because you created the table, you can change it.
text: Since you created the table, you can change it.
why: 'Since' can mean time or cause.

rewrite: Stand in line to get a donut.
text: You can't get a donut if you don't stand in line.
why: Two negatives replaced by one positive instruction.

rewrite: Select from these options: (numbered list)
text: Select from the options in the right sidebar.
why: Directional language fails when the layout changes.

identified_by: William Zinsser, On Writing Well (a university president's phrase)
rewrite: (campus protests)
text: very considerable potentially explosive expressions of dissatisfaction
why: Zinsser's example of clutter: a stack of modifiers around an abstract noun for a concrete event.

identified_by: William Zinsser, On Writing Well, ch. 16
rewrite: (Ask parents to call the teacher.)
text: (A school principal's notice about a 'special phone communication system'.)
why: Zinsser taught 40 principals four rules: clarity, simplicity, brevity, humanity.

rewrite: (A 20-word rewrite: 'the tax code', 'many methods', 'IRS errors', 'imposing personal liability on IRS employees isn't among them'.)
text: (A 34-word sentence beginning 'The Internal Revenue Code contains numerous methods...')
why: Garner estimates a line edit can cut a typical brief or contract by about 25% without changing its meaning.
